title: Struck by Lightning 7 Times: The Full Case of Ranger Roy Sullivan
description:
Case 011, the full case file. Roy Sullivan, born in Virginia in 1912, was a ranger in Shenandoah National Park in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Between 1942 and 1977 he was struck by lightning seven times and survived every strike, which Guinness World Records lists as the most lightning strikes survived by one person.

April 1942: sheltering from a storm in a fire lookout tower, he ran from it when it was hit and was struck a few steps away: a burn down his right leg, a lost big toenail and a hole in his shoe. Then 27 years with no strike. July 1969: in his truck on a mountain road, knocked unconscious, eyebrows gone. July 1970: in his own front yard, his left shoulder seared. April 1972: inside a ranger station, his hair set on fire. After that he kept water in his truck. August 1973: on patrol, his hair on fire again and his legs seared. June 1976: an injured ankle. June 1977: while fishing, burns to his chest and stomach; he was taken to hospital. His wife was also struck once, hanging out washing in their back yard while he helped her; he was not hurt that time. Two of his ranger hats, with lightning-damaged crowns, went on display in Guinness exhibit halls. He died in 1983, aged 71, and was not struck again after 1977. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The tower, road, house, yards, station, overlook, office, pond and hall in the film are generic sets, the people around him are stand-ins and not likenesses, and the cards, tags and lists are drawings made for it, not real documents. The odds figure (about 1 in 10,000 over an 80-year life) is the one Guinness World Records gives; the strikes were not independent chances, since his job kept him outdoors on high ground. If you hear thunder, get indoors or into a closed vehicle; do not shelter under trees or in open structures.

source_notes: Sources for the long version. Read in this run (15 Nov 2026): Wikipedia (Roy Sullivan) and the Guinness World Records news article of 26 January 2023 ('Incredible story of man who survived being struck by lightning SEVEN times', Vicki Newman). Not readable in this run: the Guinness record page, National Parks Traveler and The Weather Network (the fetches were refused because nobody was there to approve them, as were the Washington Post's 2013 profile, the New York Times obituary and the US National Weather Service odds page, which are therefore not used and not listed). For those first three, already sources of the Short, this film relies only on what the Short's run recorded from them on 14 Nov 2026 in episodes/r011-sullivan/episode.json; nothing new is attributed to them here. Everything the Short narrates stands as documented there. Facts added by the long version, each with where it comes from: (1) Born in Virginia in 1912: Wikipedia (7 February 1912, Greene County); consistent with Guinness news ('ex-park ranger from Virginia', died 1983 aged 71). (2) A ranger in Shenandoah National Park in the Blue Ridge Mountains: Guinness news, Wikipedia. When he started is not stated (1936 in Wikipedia, 1940 in National Parks Traveler). (3) April 1942, aged thirty: the month is in Guinness news and Wikipedia; the age is arithmetic from the birth date. (4) The tower was new and had no lightning rod: Wikipedia only, so the narration says 'by the usual account'. (5) The tower was hit and caught fire: Guinness news ('set ablaze'), The Weather Network (per the Short's notes), and Wikipedia, which reports his own description of fire jumping around inside it. (6) He ran and was struck 'a few steps from the tower': Wikipedia ('a few feet away'); Guinness news has him hit while fleeing the tower. (7) A burn down his right leg, a lost toenail, a hole in his shoe: Wikipedia (a strip along the right leg, his toe, a hole in his shoe), Guinness news (right leg scorched, big toenail lost), The Weather Network (per the Short's notes). (8) Twenty-seven years with no strike: arithmetic, 1942 to 1969, the dates of the first and second strikes in every source. Wikipedia mentions a childhood strike he never claimed; like the Short, the film leaves it out. (9) July 1969, driving his truck on a mountain road, knocked unconscious, eyebrows gone: Wikipedia and Guinness news. That a vehicle normally protects its occupants is Wikipedia's remark on this strike and standard lightning-safety advice. That the bolt came off nearby trees and in at the open window is Wikipedia only, so the narration says 'the account is that'. Left out: his hair catching fire and the truck rolling on toward a drop (Wikipedia only), and the destroyed wristwatch (Guinness news only). (10) July 1970, his front yard, left shoulder: all sources (Guinness news says 'garden'). The transformer is shown, as in the Short, not narrated. (11) April 1972, inside a ranger station, hair on fire: Guinness and Guinness news ('a guardhouse at work', April 1972), Wikipedia ('spring 1972'). (12) After the fourth strike he kept a can of water in his truck: Wikipedia (he 'began carrying a can of water' after 1972); National Parks Traveler has a container of water in his vehicle (per the Short's notes). (13) August 1973: as in the Short. Guinness news puts him 'in his vehicle'; Wikipedia and National Parks Traveler have him out of or beside it, which the film follows. (14) The nicknames: 'Human Lightning Rod' is in Wikipedia (with 'Human Lightning Conductor'), 'Spark Ranger' in Guinness news. The narration gives no date for them. (15) People keeping their distance in storms, and that it saddened him: Wikipedia only ('people were said to avoid him ... and that saddened him'), so the narration says 'it is said'. No quotation is used. (16) His wife was struck once while hanging out washing in their back yard, he was helping her and was not hurt: Wikipedia and Guinness news. Neither gives a date or says how badly she was hurt; the film gives no date, and what it shows afterwards (she sits up on the grass, he kneels by her) is dramatised. (17) June 1976: ankle injured and hair burned again: Guinness news, Wikipedia. (18) June 1977: fishing, chest and stomach burned, aged 65 (arithmetic), taken to hospital (National Parks Traveler, per the Short's notes). Guinness news says 'on a boat'; Wikipedia says a freshwater pool; the film keeps the Short's jetty and the narration says only 'fishing'. The bear-and-trout story (Wikipedia only) is left out. (19) The odds: 'about one in ten thousand' to be struck once in a long (80-year) lifetime is the figure in Guinness news and is attributed to Guinness in the narration and on the card. Other bodies give somewhat different figures. No odds are given for seven strikes: National Parks Traveler calls that sum bogus because the strikes were not independent, which is the point of Rook's line about a working life on a ridge. (20) The strikes were documented by the park superintendent, R. Taylor Hoskins, who was not present at any of them: Wikipedia only. He is not named in the film; the narration says the superintendent 'was not standing next to him at the time' and then what Guinness lists. Nothing in the film claims independent proof of each strike. (21) Two hats with lightning-damaged crowns on display in Guinness exhibit halls: Wikipedia, National Parks Traveler (per the Short's notes). (22) He died in 1983 aged 71 and was not struck again after 1977: Guinness news, Wikipedia. His death: Wikipedia and the other accounts report that he took his own life in September 1983. As in the Short, the film gives only the year and his age, says nothing of the cause and does not speculate about it; the scene is an empty bench and a clear sky. The owner should know this was a choice, made to keep the film suitable for a general audience and respectful of him. Paraphrase, not quotation: no words are attributed to anyone. The closing advice (go indoors when you hear thunder) is general safety advice, repeated in the description. Dramatised, not reported: every place (the overlook, the back yard, the office, the bench are generic sets, as are the Short's); the man at the typewriter, the two rangers who walk away and his wife are stand-ins, not likenesses, and the superintendent is not shown as any real person; what anyone wore or did beyond the sourced actions; the ranger file card, the luggage tags, the list and the dot chart (labelled in the film as drawn for it); the vehicle lights leaving the pond in 1977 (how he reached hospital is not in the sources); the weather and time of day of each scene; and everything Rook does. Rook's jokes are limited to his own reactions (the door pillar, the water can, his look at the man typing); for the people who kept away, for his wife, for the seventh strike and for his death he takes his hat off and makes none.
